neighbours.label: the object noun right after 'set the' (stage, tone, scene, table, mood): what is being set, literal or idiomatic
fire: The opening scene of the film sets the mood for everything that follows.
Early losses in the war set the stage for a long and bitter retreat.
Before guests arrived, the children set the table with the good silver.
His calm reply set the tone for the rest of the negotiation.
A short prologue sets the scene in a rainy northern port.
The lead runner set the pace for the first ten kilometers.
That first rainy week set the pattern for the whole summer.
Her keynote speech set the agenda for the three-day conference.
quiet: The opening scene of the film shows a quiet seaside town.
Early losses in the war forced a long and bitter retreat.
Before guests arrived, the children polished the good silver on the table.
His calm tone helped the rest of the negotiation go smoothly.
A short prologue describes a rainy northern port.
The lead runner kept a fast pace for the first ten kilometers.
That first rainy week ruined the whole summer for us.
Her keynote speech opened the three-day conference.

predictions: Fires on the noun right after 'set/sets/setting the'; quiet on the same nouns without 'set' before them.
notes: Probes: 'set the stage' 0.93, 'set the tone' 0.95, 'set the scene' 0.79, literal 'set the table' 0.80, 'set piece' 0.60, so it is the set + noun frame, not only the idiom. 'onto the stage' 0.01, 'The tone of his voice' 0.10; 'set the alarm' 0.27 (peak ' for').
